newsitem.title: NORWAY: Dyno sees explosives upturn, chems fall.
newsitem.headline: Dyno sees explosives upturn, chems fall.

text.p: Norway's Dyno Industrier ASA posted full-year 1996 results on Wednesday and showed an upturn in the group's explosives business but a sharp drop in profitability in chemicals.

Dyno booked an operating profit of 460 million crowns, down 24 percent from 602 million crowns in the corresponding 1995 period. Earnings before tax fell 29 percent to 373 million crowns versus 528 million crowns.
The 1995 pre-tax result included an extraordinary gain of 93 million crowns.

"The corporate result for 1996 was lower than the year before," Dyno said in a statement. "The 1996 result shows a clear improvement for Dyno's explosives business while chemicals operations experienced a setback..."

Dyno said operating profits for chemicals more than halved to 227 million crowns, including a gain of 24 million crowns from the sale of its expandable polystyrene operations, from 498 million crowns a year ago.
"The fall in profits is mainly due to considerably lower methanol prices, but also to lower margins for panelboard resins and lower sales volumes for wood adhesives," the company said.

Conversely, operating profits for explosives more than double to 228 million crowns from 91 million crowns. Dyno said the 1995 figure included a 90 million crowns provision for restructuring measures.
Operating revenues rose eight percent to 4.86 billion crowns mainly because Dyno increased its stake in its Australian explosives business, Dyno Westfarmers, to 100 percent.

The company said a sharp rise in ammonia prices -- the most important raw material in explosives production -- towards the end of the third quarter, led to short term pressure on margins. The fourth quarter had also been somewhat weaker due to seasonal fluctuations, it said.
Signs in the fourth quarter of an improvement in economic trends in the major European economies were expected to continue in 1997, Dyno said.
Profits were forecast to continue to rise in explosives as a result of improvement programmes already completed or still underway and due to expansion into new markets.

"As far as chemicals are concerned, we expect a growth in volume as a result of access to new production capacity in several markets. There are also signs that margins are returning to normal, particularly for panelboard resins," it said.
